1:
Who the descending angel is divides the witnesses. puritan-evangelical Henry judges it very probable that this angel is no other than the Lord Jesus Christ, since the description will hardly agree with any other: one who has power to bind the strong man armed and spoil his goods must be stronger than he. wesleyan-arminian Wesley draws the opposite conclusion: Jesus Christ himself overthrew the beast, but the proud dragon shall be bound by an angel, just as he and his angels were cast out of heaven by Michael and his. Clarke takes the figure as an office rather than a person, an executor of divine justice who receives criminals and keeps them in prison. reformed Gill spends his comment ruling out candidates. It is not Constantine, who cannot with any propriety be said to come down from heaven, and whose overthrow of the heathen emperors was another work altogether from binding Satan; nor an apostle or minister of the gospel, though such are called angels in this book. grammatical-historical Ellicott cuts the question off: it is needless to settle whom the angel represents, since the key and chain he carries show there is power in him who holds the keys of death and Hades to bind the one who had the power of death.

On the apparatus the notes are brief. Ellicott would render the chain as hanging from the hand rather than merely held in it, and identifies the bottomless pit with the abyss named earlier in the book, the abode of the devil and his angels. Robertson notes the word for chain is the one used of the fetter Paul wore at Rome and Peter in prison, and that the preposition means upon the hand, ready for use. Henry counts the two instruments: a great chain to bind Satan, and the key of the prison in which he is to be shut. Gill sets the scene: every other enemy removed, the devil stands alone in the way of Christ’s kingdom, and this vision tells how he will be disposed of.

Barnes prefaces the chapter with a map of it. Like the visions before it, he says, this pertains to the future, so obscurity is to be expected and only time will free its particulars from ambiguity. Two of the most formidable enemies of the church were destroyed in the previous chapter — powers he identifies as the papal and the Mohammedan — and one obstacle remains, the power of Satan concentrated in pagan form, with which the last battle is to be fought.

Among the latin-fathers, Victorinus of Pettau reads the whole passage as already in force. The years in which Satan is bound run from the first advent of Christ to the end of the age, and they are called a thousand by the manner of speech in which a part is signified by the whole, as when Scripture speaks of a word commanded for a thousand generations though they are not a thousand. As for the abyss, the devil, excluded from the hearts of believers, began to take possession of the wicked, in whose hearts, blinded day by day, he is shut up as in a profound abyss. Bede takes the vision as a recapitulation from the beginning, told more fully than before: the Lord, endued with his Father’s power, is incarnate to make war on the prince of this world and, when he is bound, to spoil his goods. He reads the names as a character sketch — dragon for malice in hurting, serpent for cunning in deceiving, devil for the fall of his estate, Satan for obstinacy in opposition — and takes the binding to mean his power was restrained from seducing men who were to be set free, since if he were permitted to exert the whole of it he would beguile most of the weak in so long a time.
2:
The seizure is described with a word of force. grammatical-historical Barnes notes that the verb means to lay hold by violence, and that it implies a power superior to the dragon’s own; the great enemy is himself mighty and can be overcome only by a greater, which may teach that only a power from heaven can destroy the empire of Satan in the world. reformed Gill is careful about the identification. The dragon here is not Paganism, for that was destroyed in the Roman empire under the sixth seal and will be destroyed elsewhere under the vials, when the kings of the earth gathered at Armageddon are slain and the cities of the nations fall, Papal and Mahometan alike; the devil himself is intended, so called for the power and cruelty he has exercised and for the venom of idolatry, superstition and false worship with which he has infected the inhabitants of the earth. Ellicott takes the four titles together as a portrait: fierce as the dragon, subtle as the serpent, the slanderer of God and his people, and the adversary of all righteousness. Robertson observes that the words are exactly those of the earlier vision, except that the nominative is retained here in apposition with the accusative, a grammatical break of a kind frequent in this book, and that he who has stood behind the beast and the false prophet from the start is now himself seized.

The thousand years divide the witnesses more sharply than the binding does. wesleyan-arminian Clarke doubts anyone can tell in what the binding consists, and says that the passage refers to a time in which the influence of Satan will be greatly restrained and the true Church enjoy long prosperity; but he refuses a literal count, since it is not likely that this one number should be taken literally while every other year in the book is symbolic. He adds that the expectation has been idle in every century since the Christian era, fixed for several different years within his own lifetime, and that he believed those predictions vain and lived to see them so. Ellicott notes that a thousand years was the length at which the Rabbis fixed the duration of Messiah’s kingdom, and that the period symbolises a lengthened time rather than a measured one. Robertson finds here the same problem as the twelve hundred and sixty days, and offers the apostolic saying that one day with the Lord is as a thousand years and a thousand years as one day (2 Peter 3:8), adding that the book was written to comfort saints in a time of great trial, not to create strife among them. Wesley argues the contrary case in five steps: the thousand years wholly follow the times of the beast rather than running parallel with them, as the unbroken chain of events in the book shows, as the sequence of the dragon’s casting down, raging, imprisonment, loosing and final destruction shows, and above all because these years bring a full and lasting immunity from all outward and inward evils together with an affluence of all blessings — and such a time the church has never yet seen, and it is therefore still to come.
4:
The thrones are seen before their occupants are named, and the witnesses fill the gap differently. grammatical-historical Barnes keeps to what the text says: the seer reports thrones with persons sitting on them and does not intimate who they were, nor how many the thrones were; the plural rules out the throne of God, and the clause that follows shows they were placed with reference to a judgment, as in the prophet’s vision where he looked until the thrones were set (Daniel 7:9). Robertson notes that the plural verb is given no subject at all, and offers the candidates — Christ and the apostles as promised (Matthew 19:28), some of the saints (1 Corinthians 6:3), the martyrs as others hold — calling the scene a picture of the heavenly court of assizes. Ellicott answers the question from the verse itself: those said in the latter half to reign with Christ are the same who sit on the thrones that first caught the seer’s eye, and they are all the real servants of God, appearing in two classes. First the martyrs faithful unto death, the beheaded standing for the whole company; then those faithful in life, whoever did not worship the beast or his image or take his mark. Whatever the triumph and sovereignty are, they are shared by all the faithful. reformed Gill agrees that thrones are pitched for all the saints, who sit as kings and conquerors, quiet and undisturbed; after the binding of Satan an account is given of their happiness during that time. wesleyan-arminian Wesley alone insists that those on the thrones are distinguished both from the souls mentioned immediately after and from the saints already raised, though who and how many they are is not said.

On the manner of death the notes converge. Robertson observes that the participle comes from the word for an axe, the traditional instrument of execution in republican Rome afterwards supplanted by the sword, and that it occurs nowhere else in the New Testament; Wesley says the same and adds that one kind of death particularly inflicted at Rome stands for all, the martyrs being killed sometimes for the word of God in general, while they refused to worship idols, and sometimes for the testimony of Jesus, while they confessed his name. The reigning divides them again. Wesley reads it as souls and bodies reunited, and reigning with Christ not on earth but in heaven, the reigning on earth spoken of earlier in the book being quite a different thing (Revelation 11:15). Clarke reads the thrones as Christianity established in the earth, the kings and governors being all Christians, and the period as a long undisturbed prosperity in which the Gospel spirit prevails so universally that it will appear as if Christ reigned on earth — which will in effect be the case, since his Spirit shall rule in the hearts of men; the martyrs live again in that their testimony is revived and the truth they died for is everywhere prevalent. He treats the phrase itself as rabbinical, tracing the thousand years of Messiah’s days through Jewish tradition. puritan-evangelical Henry expects a thousand years to follow the destruction of the antichristian and persecuting powers, during which pure Christianity in doctrine, worship and holiness will be made known over all the earth, fallen man being new-created by the all-powerful working of the Holy Spirit, so that faith and holiness shall as certainly prevail as unbelief now does. Robertson leaves the verb open: an ingressive aorist would mean they came to life, a constative one an increased spiritual life, the double sense of life and death running through the Gospel as well (John 5:21-29).
5:
Who is left out of the first resurrection is the hinge, and the readings do not agree on so much as the class of persons meant. reformed Gill takes the rest of the dead to be the wicked dead and no others, since the saints will all be raised together, and to be dead here in the bodily sense rather than the moral or spiritual one. grammatical-historical Barnes reads the phrase the other way about, as most naturally referring to the same general class already in view — the pious dead. On his account the martyrs would be honoured as if they were raised up and the others not: special respect would be shown to their principles, their memory and their character, so that an eminent piety would be exalted above the common and ordinary piety of the church. The rest of the pious dead would indeed be raised and rewarded, but would occupy comparatively humble places, as though they did not share the exalted triumphs of the world’s subjection to the Saviour; they did not come into remembrance, and their principles were not what then characterised the church. Robertson reports both options without choosing — all except the martyrs, righteous and unrighteous alike, or else only the wicked — and warns against the inference that the living of the previous verse must therefore be a bodily resuscitation, since that is to interpret apocalyptic prophecy by methods of exegesis proper to ordinary narrative. He confesses his own ignorance of the symbolism and disclaims any predilection for either millennial scheme.

Ellicott names the stakes outright: here is one of the keys to the whole controversy. It has been argued that resurrection must be understood literally, and that the contrasting clause forces it; but there is no reason to restrict the word to a literal meaning, since the sacred writers use the idea figuratively of the dead in sin summoned to rise that Christ may give them light (Ephesians 2:1), and the figure often underlies their language and their arguments (Romans 6:5). If the words lived not necessarily mean that the rest of the dead did not enjoy physical life on earth, then the saints’ living must mean physical life on earth too — and he denies that the reader is bound to either. Clarke states the common supposition, that all who were martyred shall be raised a thousand years before the other dead and reign on earth with Christ, and adds only that this also is very doubtful. Robertson notes further that scholars differ over whether the closing sentence about the first resurrection is genuine at all; taken as genuine it has been applied to the return of the martyrs and confessors to life at the beginning of the period, making it an incident within the present life rather than a parallel to the raising of the dead in Christ (1 Thessalonians 4:16), while others find in it the regeneration and the restoration promised elsewhere (Acts 3:21). He sets against it the general judgment out of the books later in the chapter and the general resurrection of the just and the unjust (Acts 24:15). wesleyan-arminian Wesley cuts the knot with chronology instead: two distinct thousands are in view throughout, the one in which Satan is bound beginning and ending much sooner than the other, and neither boundary knowable to men on earth, since both the imprisonment and the loosing are transacted in the invisible world. By observing the two, he says, prophecies that seemed to clash are reconciled — those promising a most flourishing state of the church yet to come, and those describing the fatal security of men in the last days.
6:
The verse is a benediction, and the witnesses take up its two halves in turn. grammatical-historical Robertson counts it the fifth of the book’s beatitudes, with two more still to come and seven in all, and notes that here the word holy is added to the usual blessed. Ellicott reads the blessing as having one definite feature: on these the second death has no authority. That death stands in contrast with the first resurrection and is not mere physical dying but the more awful death lying outside the region of things seen and temporal, spiritual rather than bodily; and it is not the life of the body that protects the life of the spirit, but the living and believing in God, according to the word spoken of such, that they shall never die (John 11:26). Barnes glosses blessed as happy or favoured, a word designed to support those who in the seer’s own time suffered persecution or might suffer it afterwards, and holy as meaning that none will be thus honoured who lacks an established character for sanctity: holy principles will reign then, and no other kind of person will be exalted. He defines the second death as the death the wicked experience in the world of woe, and calls it a blessed state indeed which enjoys absolute security against death in any and every form, since we know what death is here and are told of the bitter pains of the other. wesleyan-arminian Clarke agrees on the word — happy — and explains the pairing historically: he was holy, and therefore he suffered for the testimony of Jesus at a time when nothing but holiness was called to such a trial. He takes the first resurrection to be that of the martyrs, and the second death to be punishment in the eternal world, which he says is the acceptation of the phrase among the ancient Jews; the idiom of having no power, that is no authority or dominion, he likewise traces to rabbinical usage.

On who is included the accounts diverge. reformed Gill offers the clause as either a description of the persons or of their condition. As description, it marks out only those blessed with spiritual blessings — with a justifying righteousness, pardon of sin and regenerating grace, sanctified by the Spirit of God — and these only will be first raised and called to inherit the kingdom prepared for them; as a statement of their condition, it means they shall be perfectly blessed in soul and body and perfectly holy in both. Ellicott widens the circle rather than narrowing it: theirs is the priesthood of life who have offered themselves a living sacrifice to God (Romans 12:1), and the kingship of life belongs to those who have overcome the world-powers in the word of God and in the blood of the Lamb; these truly reign. Robertson admits the passage raises the question whether the first and the second resurrections are both of the body or one of them of the spirit, and says there seems no way to reach a solid conception of it, noting that one apostle mentions the raising only of those who are Christ’s (1 Corinthians 15:23) yet elsewhere speaks of the just and the unjust as if one event. He observes too that where the book earlier promised the saints should reign upon the earth, that item does not appear here, so that no hint is given as to where the service is to be rendered or the royalty exercised. Wesley draws one inference and no more: they shall be priests of God and of Christ — therefore Christ is God. Barnes, opening his long excursus at this point, grants that this is the principal passage relied upon by those who advocate a literal reign of Christ upon the earth.
7:
The loosing is stated without a reason, and the witnesses feel it. grammatical-historical Barnes says plainly that no intimation is given why or how Satan would be released, and warns against inferring a merely arbitrary act on the part of God; all that need be supposed is a temporary outbreak of wickedness in certain parts of the world, as if Satan were for a time let loose again. Ellicott reads binding and loosing as restraint imposed and restraint removed, and treats the intervening reign as an opportunity that must at last close: it has been a witness to Christ’s power over the wicked one and the earthly approximation to the ideal picture, but the lament over Israel’s refusal to hearken has its counterpart over earth’s lost opportunities. Christendom, he says, is planted to be a framework of regenerating power to mankind as the Law was in Israel; and as there the old idolatrous influences broke in upon the rule of the covenant, so here the vision pictures Christendom invaded by the evil one once mankind has let slip a really golden age. wesleyan-arminian Clarke presses the sequence as an argument: how can this bear any kind of literal interpretation? Satan is bound, the earth is at peace, righteousness flourishes, and Christ alone reigns — a state that might continue for ever if the imprisonment did; yet he is loosed, peace is banished, and a dreadful war follows. These can be only symbolical representations, utterly incapable of the sense generally put upon them. Wesley notes instead that Satan goes forth the more diligently for having been so long restrained and knowing his time is short. reformed Gill argues that the years are not yet expired by ruling out the dates proposed for their close: not the year 1000, nor 1033 reckoned from the birth or death of Christ, when Paganism was brought into the church that bore the Christian name — for that had been entering by degrees long before, so that Satan was already loose; nor 1073 reckoned from the destruction of Jerusalem, when there came to the popedom a man he calls the brand of hell, who raised the papal power over princes and made the see of Rome independent. puritan-evangelical Henry draws the moral: while this world lasts Satan’s power will be limited and lessened but not wholly destroyed, and it would be well if the servants of Christ were as active in doing good as his enemies in doing mischief.

On the two names the accounts nearly agree, parting only at the end. Ellicott derives them from the earlier prophet, notes that rabbinical books used them for the nations that would rise against Messiah’s reign, and insists they are figurative, since no particular nation could well be called the nations in the four corners of the earth; the memory of the northern invasions lingered long in Asiatic minds, and those names came to represent the great and undefined enemies who would in after ages assail the kingdom. Robertson traces them to the same prophet, reports that some early Christian writers thought of the Goths and Huns while others refused to narrow the imagery and saw only the final protest of the world against Christianity, and draws the sharpest inference in the chapter: the millennium, whatever it is, cannot mean a period when Satan has no following on earth, since this vast host rallies at once to his standard. Barnes adds that the deception is not confined to one portion of the world, and that though the gospel would then generally prevail, the native character of the human heart would not be changed. Wesley alone keeps the names concrete: Magog is the father of the innumerable northern nations toward the east, Gog their prince, both names signifying high or lifted up; when that fierce leader appears, then will his own name be known.
9:
The invasion is described as an army on the march, and the witnesses take the geography differently. grammatical-historical Barnes sees extended columns spreading over a land, and says no literal armies summoned from regions actually called by those names need be supposed; what is implied is a hostility to the church well pictured by an invading host of barbarians. He notes that the phrase about the breadth of the land is used of the Chaldean invasion and there means the whole extent of it (Habakkuk 1:6), and that the besiegers could compass the camp and encircle the city at once, which shows their numbers; the camp he takes to lie outside the walls, an army drawn out to defend. reformed Gill allows either the whole earth or the land of Israel where Christ and his people will be, so that the risen wicked come up from every part of the world and spread over the holy land as the earlier prophet’s host covers Israel like a cloud; the phrase for the breadth of the land is used elsewhere of Immanuel’s land. Ellicott has the multitudes spread like swarms, and identifies the beloved city as Jerusalem, in which was the mount that God loved (Psalm 78:68), figure of the true spiritual Zion faithful to her king. The city has its camp because it is ready for war; its citizens, like the exiles who rebuilt the wall, could never lay down the sword (Nehemiah 4:17-18). Robertson glosses the camp as the ordinary word for a military encampment, used in the Greek Old Testament of Israel in the desert and in the New Testament of Roman barracks and of an army in line of battle, and reports the division over the city — some taking it for Jerusalem, others for the Church. wesleyan-arminian Clarke settles it in a line: the beloved city is primarily Jerusalem, typically the Christian Church. Wesley makes the camp the gentile church dwelling round about Jerusalem.

The fire ends the siege before it is fought. Ellicott says the demonstration is arrested by divine act, and reads the descending flame as the light that tabernacled over the holy city, ready to break forth upon the wicked; he hears in it the overthrow of the cities of the plain (Genesis 19:24), the fire that fell on an earlier prophet’s enemies (2 Kings 1:10) and the fire that broke from the tabernacle upon those who defied the law, and insists these are used as imagery — figurative, though not empty figure, for Christ will thoroughly purge his floor (Matthew 3:12). Robertson calls it a vivid climax to this last great battle with Satan. Barnes marks the symmetry of what follows: the beast and the false prophet had been cast alive into the lake, while Satan was confined for a season in a dark abyss instead, and now receives the same, so that the enemies associated in deceiving the nations share one punishment. With that, he says, every great enemy of the church is destroyed, the gospel triumphs, and the way is prepared for the final consummation. Ellicott traces the descent by stages — cast from heaven, bound in the abyss, now flung into the flaming lake — and observes that with the three enemies driven from the earth they sought to destroy, the judgment of human beings must follow. Clarke marks the change of degree: before, Satan was bound and his power curtailed; now it is totally taken away. Gill notes that the devil deceived these nations twice over, in the present life by drawing them into profaneness or false worship or persecution, and afterwards by instigating this last foolish attempt. Wesley reads the torment as unremitting: day and night, that is without any intermission — though strictly there is only night there, no day, no sun, no hope.
11:
The throne is described by two adjectives, and both carry weight. grammatical-historical Barnes takes great to mean high or elevated, on the pattern of the throne high and lifted up (Isaiah 6:1), and white to mean splendid or shining, and identifies the seat with what is elsewhere called the throne of his glory (Matthew 25:31). Ellicott hears the two words as a deliberate contrast with the book’s other thrones: white in token of the purity of the judgment that follows, since he who sits upon it is of purer eyes than to behold iniquity. Robertson makes the same point: the absolute purity of this supreme court is symbolised by the colour, as where the garment was white as snow (Daniel 7:9). wesleyan-arminian Clarke calls it refulgent with glorious majesty. puritan-evangelical Henry reads the placing of the scene as an argument: the destruction of the devil’s kingdom properly leads to the day of judgment, and we may be assured there will be one when we see that the prince of this world is judged (John 16:11). The tribunal is glorious and perfectly righteous; the throne of iniquity that establishes wickedness by a law has no fellowship with it. reformed Gill spends his note refusing an application: the vision does not refer to the Gospel dispensation running from the exaltation of Christ to his second coming, though that period had its own shaking of heaven and earth, its own removal of the Mosaic economy and of Paganism, and its own opening of the books, the book of life being disclosed by the conversion of some and not others.

Who occupies it divides them. Barnes says the reference is undoubtedly to the Lord Jesus Christ as final Judge, and the scene his second advent; Wesley names him as plainly, adding that the apostle does not describe him. Clarke names the indescribable Jehovah instead. Ellicott holds both together: throughout the book God is the one who sits upon the throne, but this must not be understood as excluding the Son, who sits with his Father on his throne and who as Son of Man declared that he would divide all the nations as a shepherd divides the sheep from the goats. Robertson resolves it from the other end: the name of God is not mentioned, but the Almighty Father sits there, and the Son sits with him and works with him (John 5:19-21). On the flight of earth and heaven the question is how much is asserted. Wesley presses the language hardest: probably both the aerial and starry heaven are meant, and both were wholly dissolved — it is not said they were thrown into commotions but that they fled entirely away, not that they started from their foundations but that they fell into dissolution, not that they removed to a distant place but that there was found no place for them. And all this, he adds, not at any command or fiery indignation, but at the bare presence of a Majesty sitting in severe but adorable dignity. Clarke agrees that the brightness of the countenance dissolved the universe and annihilated the laws governing it. Barnes softens it to appearance: as the stars at sunrise seem to flee to remoter regions and vanish, so at the descent of the Son of God the earth and all other worlds shall seem to vanish. Robertson notes only that the non-eternity of matter is common teaching in both Testaments. Ellicott enters the caveat: some have read the verse of putting away the irrational creation pressed into the service of sin, others of the destruction of the whole visible world, but the book’s earlier imagery should make us cautious of asserting that any physical catastrophe is described, for revolution must precede renewal and it is never safe to ground expectations on language confessedly poetical in form.
12:
The identity of the dead who stand before the throne is the chapter’s sharpest disagreement, and follows from what each made of the first resurrection. grammatical-historical Barnes takes the phrase to mean all the dead without remainder, small and great being one of those pairs — like young and old, bond and free, righteous and wicked — that divide the whole race; and he presses the consequence, that this precludes any previous raising of part of the dead at the start of the thousand years. There is no intimation, he insists, that only the wicked dead are meant, and the same follows from the surrender by sea and death, which he calls inconsistent with the supposition that a large part of the dead had already risen to reign in glorified bodies. reformed Gill reads it in the opposite sense: these are the rest of the dead, the wicked, who lived not again until the thousand years were ended, for the righteous were judged at their own resurrection at the beginning of the day of the Lord and will have held the kingdom a thousand years by the time these are raised. Small and great he refers to age or to condition, kings and peasants. Robertson notes that the general resurrection of the following verse is pictured by anticipation as already over, and that no living are mentioned, though some will be living when Christ comes to judge the quick and the dead. wesleyan-arminian Wesley makes room for those, adding that the dead of every age and condition includes also such as undergo a change equivalent to death (1 Corinthians 15:51).

On the books there is more agreement, and one qualification. Barnes takes them for the record of human deeds, the imagery drawn from accusations made against those arraigned before human courts, the record forming its basis. Robertson says the record of each human being has been kept in God’s books, so the sentence upon each rests on written evidence, and calls the other book the roll of living citizens, the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven; the books are the vouchers for the book of life, and though we are saved by grace, character at last is the test, as the fruit is of the tree. Clarke identifies the two as the book of life and the book of death, the account of men’s good and evil actions, traces the imagery to the earlier prophet whose opened books underlie the rabbinical accounts as well (Daniel 7:10), and calls the expressions figurative in both. He then qualifies: judgment is according to their works, and according to their faith also, for the works would prove whether the faith were true or false — but faith by itself could be no rule in such a procedure. Wesley contrasts these with the books of human judges, written with pen and ink, and observes that it is not said they will be read: the light of that day will make them visible to all. With the book of God’s omniscience that of conscience will exactly tally, the natural law as well as the revealed will be displayed, every man will know himself with the last exactness, and this will be the first true, impartial and universal history; the other book holds all who are accepted through the Beloved, all who lived and died in the faith that worketh by love. On the surrender of the dead Gill insists the sea is literal, not a figure for the troubled world, and thinks particularly of those drowned in the flood; Clarke divides the custody — sea and death hold the bodies, hades the spirits, and since judgment requires both, each gives up what it kept. Robertson notes that some do read the sea as that of a troubled and sinful world, and that death and hades are an inseparable pair.
14:
What it means for death and hades to be cast into the lake is a difficulty, felt most by the reader who takes the terms literally. reformed Gill states the problem outright: death cannot be taken properly here, nor hell be the place of torment, since that place is itself the lake of fire, and the sense would then be that hell is cast into hell. He canvasses the possibilities — the devil, who has the power of death and is prince of hell, except that his casting in has just been narrated; or the abolition of death and the grave, so that they should no more have power over men; or rather, he concludes, the wicked dead they delivered up, now sentenced to eternal death. grammatical-historical Barnes reads it as the fulfilment of the promise that the last enemy destroyed is death (1 Corinthians 15:26): death as the separation of soul and body will exist no more, the righteous living for ever and the wicked lingering in a state death never ends. There would still be death, but of another kind — not a separation of soul and body but a continual agony, like the first in intensity though not in kind. He turns this into an argument: since a second death is described as still existing, the casting in of death and hades cannot mean that all punishment ceases and all are saved. wesleyan-arminian Clarke draws it in his own terms. The first death consisted in the separation of the soul from the body for a season, the second in the separation of body and soul from God for ever; the first admits a resurrection, the second none; by the first the body is destroyed during time, by the second body and soul through eternity. Death himself, he adds, is abolished and the place for separate spirits no longer needful, since bodies and souls are rejoined and no further separation will take place. Wesley says it in a sentence: they were abolished for ever, for neither righteous nor wicked were to die any more. Robertson lets the note become a doxology: death is personified and disposed of, the apostle’s song of victory answered, hades has no more terrors since the saints are in heaven, and there is no more fear of death because death is no more.

The closing verse is the chapter’s verdict, stated by each in his own register. Barnes dwells on the word’s comprehensiveness: no term could be wider, and the single condition on which anyone escapes is that he is found written in the book of life. All the rest — princes and nobles, philosophers, statesmen and conquerors, rich and poor, bond and free, young and aged, proud and humble — will be doomed alike; unlike in every other thing, they are alike in the one thing on which their destiny depends. Clarke reaches for the civic register. Those whose names were not found in the public rolls, either because they were never citizens or because their names had been erased for crimes against the state, could claim none of a citizen’s privileges; and so those who did not belong to the new and spiritual Jerusalem, or had forfeited their privileges by sin, were cast into the lake. He turns to direct address: see that thy name be written in the sacred register, and, if written in, see that it never be blotted out. Robertson draws boundaries instead: this short sentence tells the doom of all who are out of Christ, and leaves no room for soul sleeping, an intermediate state, a second chance, or the annihilation of the wicked, since Scripture knows a resurrection to death as well as to life (John 5:29). Gill names those the opened book will not contain: all that worship the beast and wonder after him, and all wicked men, every one of them.
